name: In-office laser whitening
lead: In-office laser whitening is a professional tooth-bleaching procedure in which a peroxide gel is applied to the teeth and a light source, described by providers as a laser, LED or diode unit, is directed at it to accelerate the colour change.[1][3] It is delivered by dental staff, with the gums protected by a barrier, and is one of several light-activated in-office options.[1]

Reviews have examined whether the light adds anything. A 2019 systematic review and network meta-analysis asked whether any light-activation protocol improves colour change when combined with an in-office gel.[2] Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article reports that light activation may not outperform high-concentration peroxide alone and that a 2015 study found no improvement and a possible rise in tissue temperature.[1]
Tooth sensitivity is the most commonly reported side effect of in-office bleaching.[1]
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide gel, roughly 25-38% in power-bleaching systems[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes in-office bleaching as involving a light-cured barrier on the gums and papillae, followed by a high-strength peroxide gel; power-bleaching gels contain about 25-38% hydrogen peroxide, and light exposure runs roughly 6-15 minutes.[1] Cosmetic-dentistry descriptions mention a rubber dam over the gums and an argon laser to speed the process, and one such description claims it is several times more effective than other methods without giving a source.[3] Only dental professionals may administer these products in many jurisdictions.[1]

Wikipedia reports that in-office bleaching often produces a change of 2 to 7 shades and can last several months, with yellow teeth responding best and grey teeth least; it also notes that a large share of the change from a one-hour treatment may rebound within a week.[1] Whether light adds benefit remains debated: the network meta-analysis was designed to compare light-activation systems against gel alone,[2] while Wikipedia cites findings that light did not improve results.[1]

Wikipedia reports that 67-78% of in-office patients experience sensitivity lasting roughly 4-39 days, and that high-concentration peroxide can irritate mucous membranes and burn gums if unprotected.[1] It also notes that light can raise tissue temperature.[1] Several registered trials have studied lasers or photobiomodulation as a way to reduce post-whitening sensitivity.[4][5]

A two-year split-mouth study of 48 patients compared in-office bleaching with and without light activation (35% hydrogen peroxide with a hybrid LED/diode laser) against other bleaching techniques, measuring colour change, stability and sensitivity.[6] A 2019 systematic review and network meta-analysis compared light-activation protocols used with in-office gel.[2] Registered trials include studies of laser versus chemical whitening and of lasers for whitening sensitivity.[4][5][7]

card.summary: Peroxide gel on the teeth with a light or laser to speed it up; whether the light adds anything beyond the gel is still contested.
card.note: Sensitivity is common; colour can partly rebound.

quick.overview:
In-office laser whitening is a dentist-delivered bleaching treatment where a strong peroxide gel is applied and a light or laser unit is aimed at the teeth. Whitening itself is supported by studies; the extra role of the light is debated.

Wikipedia reports typical changes of 2 to 7 shades that can last months, with some rebound in the first week.
quick.mechanism: The peroxide gel breaks down stain molecules inside the tooth. Light or laser units are marketed as accelerating that reaction, though a network meta-analysis and other studies have examined whether they improve results over gel alone.
quick.risks: Sensitivity is reported by most patients in some studies, lasting days to weeks. Unprotected gums can be burned by strong gels, and heat from light is a reported concern. It is generally provided only by dental professionals.
